strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored evaluation setting: end-to-end data-to-insight pipelines over realistic, dirty, multi-file data lakes, going beyond prior benchmarks (DS-1000, BLADE, DSBench, ScienceAgentBench) that test individual steps or preprocessed data. The comparison table (Table 1) against prior benchmarks is informative and largely convincing.

The benchmark itself is substantial: 104 manually curated tasks with 633 subtasks, 1700+ data files from 24 public sources across 6 diverse domains, with reference solutions, key functionalities, and ground-truth answers released. The three-tier evaluation design (end-to-end automation, pipeline design, pipeline implementation) is sensible and provides diagnostic value beyond a single headline metric.

Task validation is reasonably careful: independent annotator reconstruction of pipelines, multi-pass verification of specifications and reference solutions, and typed scoring schemes (exact/approximate string, numeric, list) tailored to answer types.

Comprehensive system evaluation (18 DS-GURU/model combinations plus Deep Research and Gemini 2.5) with per-domain breakdowns and informative failure-mode analysis (e.g., wildfire domain leakage from parametric knowledge, astronomy's low scores due to custom formats, print-debugging causing structural drift).

Overall findings are meaningful and well-supported: out-of-the-box LLMs fall short on realistic data-to-insight work despite competence on well-specified code generation, which motivates future work on data science agents.
weaknesses: The manuscript is not camera-ready quality and contains internal inconsistencies that undermine confidence: the abstract says '5 general models and 3 code generation models' while Section 5.1 lists 6 models; the contribution list says '21 real-world data sources' while Table 2/7 and the abstract say 24; contribution (4) contains a literal placeholder 'XX real-world systems'; a sentence ends mid-word ('Artifacts ... are available a'). Table 2 and Table 7 are duplicates.

Table 8 (fine-grained results) appears to be a stale artifact from a different experimental setup: it lists models (GPT-4o-mini, GLM-4-Flash, Gemma2-9Bit) that are not described anywhere in the experimental setup, has many blank cells including missing 'Overall' scores, and is not referenced or explained. This is a serious reproducibility and reporting flaw.

The Deep Research / Gemini comparison (Table 5) is not apples-to-apples and the authors themselves concede the evaluation is compromised: inputs were pre-filtered to at most 10 files guaranteed to contain the relevant data (defeating the core data-discovery challenge), and Deep Research could not be prevented from web-scraping answers that may come from the very papers/reports the tasks were derived from. The 52% vs 22% comparison should therefore be treated as anecdotal, but the paper draws conclusions from it.

Contamination concerns are acknowledged but not resolved: wildfire tasks are answerable from parametric knowledge (naive DS-GURU gets 24.87% with no data supplied), and the legal tasks derive from public dashboards/reports. The paper reports these numbers without decontaminated or leakage-adjusted analysis.

The pipeline design metric relies on LLM-as-judge (CodeJudge-style) with manually curated key functionalities; no validation of the judge's agreement with human judgment is reported, so the design scores (the largest differentiator in Table 6) have uncertain reliability.

Domain and difficulty distribution is uneven (9 biomedical tasks vs 30 legal), 'easy vs hard' is a crude binary based on file count and subtask count, and with only 104 tasks per-domain conclusions rest on very few tasks.

DS-GURU is a fairly minimal single-model decomposition baseline; evaluation of more sophisticated agentic designs over the full (unfiltered) data lake is absent, so the benchmark's discriminative power among strong agent architectures remains untested.

strengths: The problem is well-motivated and relevant: end-to-end data-to-insight pipelines over messy, heterogeneous data lakes is a real gap compared to existing code generation, text-to-SQL, and data analysis benchmarks.
The benchmark is based on real-world data sources across 6 domains, with manually implemented and validated reference solutions, and independent re-annotation of tasks to reduce ambiguity.
The three-tier evaluation design (end-to-end automation, pipeline design, pipeline implementation) provides diagnostic insight beyond a single aggregate score.
The paper provides a clear comparison table against related benchmarks and releases tasks, reference solutions, and a baseline framework.
weaknesses: Severe presentation and consistency problems that undermine confidence in the work: the contributions list contains a literal placeholder ('we evaluate the capabilities of XX real-world systems'), URLs are truncated/missing (e.g., 'available at' with no link), and the model counts are inconsistent (abstract claims 5 general + 3 code generation models; experiments use 6 models; Table 8 lists yet another set including GPT-4o-mini, GLM-4-Flash, Gemma2-9Bit that never appear elsewhere).

Table 8 is largely empty (most rows have no values) and references '24 methods' with undefined metrics ('Overall' column missing values), and the corresponding fine-grained metrics are never explained in the text; several numbers contradict Table 4/6 (e.g., DeepSeek-R1 self-correcting total reported as 6.34% vs 6.35%).

Appendix D is unfinished: 'For each level of Level 3 - The COMPLETE mode.' is a dangling sentence, and the Level 1/2/3 COMPLETE/PLAN/ASSIST mode taxonomy appears only in the appendix and conflicts with the 'end-to-end/pipeline design/implementation' framing in the main text.

The benchmark has a demonstrated contamination/shortcut problem that the authors themselves admit: wildfire tasks are solved well even in the 'naive' setting with no data, because answers are recoverable from parametric knowledge or web scraping (OpenAI Deep Research was allowed to scrape and possibly fetch answers from the very papers the tasks were derived from). No decontamination strategy or mitigation is offered, casting doubt on what the headline scores measure.

Evaluation reliability is under-supported: the pipeline design setting relies on an LLM judge (CodeJudge-style) for binary functionality decisions without reporting judge validation, inter-annotator agreement with human judgment, or agreement statistics; no confidence intervals, variance over runs, or statistical significance are provided despite non-deterministic LLM calls.

The comparison between DS-GURU and commercial systems is unfair and poorly controlled: Deep Research and Gemini are given pre-filtered input files (guaranteed to contain the answer files) plus internet access, while DS-GURU sees the full lake; conclusions about relative capability are not interpretable under these differing conditions.

DS-GURU itself is a very thin baseline (single-shot prompting with snippet sampling and up to 5 self-correction iterations) with no ablations on key design choices (N for sampling, number of iterations, prompt variants), limiting the paper's analytical claims about why models fail.

Many empirical claims are asserted from qualitative impressions ('models rely on print debugging', 'structural drift') without supporting quantitative analysis, examples, or error taxonomy; the failure-mode analysis promised in Section 1 is essentially absent.
Data/file scale claims are inconsistent (104 tasks over '1700 data files from 24 sources' in the abstract vs '21 data sources' in the contributions; Table 2 totals 1764 datasets).

Overall, the manuscript reads as a draft rather than a finished submission, with unfinished sections, placeholder text, empty tables, and irreconcilable numbers across sections, making the central claims (benchmark quality and evaluation validity) insufficiently supported in its current form.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: existing data science benchmarks (DS-1000, ARCADE, BLADE, DSBench) test isolated steps, while KRamaBench evaluates end-to-end data-to-insight pipelines over large, messy, multi-file data lakes, which better reflects real-world data science practice.
The benchmark is substantial and grounded in reality: 104 manually curated tasks spanning 6 domains, ~1700 data files from 24 real public sources, with reference solutions and 633 sub-tasks.

The validation methodology for task quality is reasonable: independent annotators reconstructing pipelines, resolution of ambiguities, ground-truth answers for both end tasks and sub-tasks, and a well-defined scoring scheme across six answer types (Table 3).

The multi-granularity evaluation design (end-to-end automation, pipeline design, pipeline implementation) provides useful diagnostic insight into failure modes, and the finding that models show better design than implementation capability, and that self-correction yields diminishing returns in well-scoped settings, is an interesting empirical observation.

Baseline evaluation is reasonably broad (multiple LLM backbones across three DS-GURU variants), plus manual evaluation of agentic services (OpenAI Deep Research, Gemini 2.5 Pro), with cost/runtime reporting.
The paper is transparent about contamination risks (wildfire domain answers in parametric knowledge; Deep Research web access), and publishes artifacts, which supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: The manuscript has serious signs of being an unfinished draft: a placeholder 'XX real-world systems' in the contribution list, truncated sentences ('available a', missing repository URLs), grammar errors ('can design, implementation, and execute'), and duplicated tables (Table 2 = Table 7). These undermine confidence in overall care and polish.

Inconsistent numbers throughout: 24 data sources in the abstract vs. '21 real-world data sources' in the contributions; '5 general models and 3 code generation models' in the abstract vs. 6 models in Section 5.1 vs. '8 different systems' in the conclusion; Section 5.4 attributes 22.08% to GPT-4o self-correcting when that figure belongs to GPT-o3 (GPT-4o is 8.28%).

Appendix D ('Level 1/2/3 COMPLETE/PLAN/ASSIST modes') describes an evaluation taxonomy that does not match the three settings defined in Section 3 (end-to-end automation, pipeline design, pipeline implementation) and appears to be leftover material from a different draft, confusing the reader about the actual benchmark protocol.

Table 8 ('Fine-grained evaluation results on 24 methods') uses a completely different model set (GPT-4o-mini, GLM-4-Flash, Gemma2-9Bit) that is never introduced, has many empty cells, and is never discussed in the text; it seems imported from an unrelated evaluation and should be removed or explained.

Benchmark validity concerns from data contamination are significant rather than incidental: wildfire tasks are solvable from parametric knowledge even in the naive setting with no data (explaining the anomalously high 24.87% for GPT-o3), and OpenAI Deep Research could not be prevented from web-scraping (52.18% vs. 8.47% in Table 4 under different conditions), weakening headline comparisons involving these systems.

Pipeline design evaluation relies on an LLM-as-judge (CodeJudge-style) against human-annotated key functionalities; no validation of judge reliability (agreement with human judgments) is reported, yet design scores drive several qualitative claims.

The benchmark is relatively small (104 tasks, concentrated in legal with 30 tasks) and difficulty categorization ('easy'/'hard' by subtask count and file count) is heuristic; per-difficulty results are never reported despite introducing the split.

The DS-GURU baseline is a fairly straightforward chain-of-thought + retry prompting pipeline; its novelty as a contribution is limited, and no comparison to existing agentic data-science systems (e.g., DS-Agent, AutoPrep) is provided on the benchmark.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and timely gap: existing data-science benchmarks (DS-1000, DSBench, BLADE, ScienceAgentBench) test isolated steps, while KramaBench targets end-to-end data-lake-to-insight pipelines with real, heterogeneous, unclean data (1700 files, 24 sources, 6 domains), a setting clearly closer to real-world data science.

Careful and thorough benchmark construction methodology: tasks grounded in published studies, a 4-step curation workflow with cross-contributor validation, reference pipelines, key functionalities, and 633 annotated sub-tasks with ground-truth answers.

A well-designed, multi-level evaluation framework (end-to-end automation, pipeline design, sub-task implementation) that separates retrieval failures from reasoning/implementation failures via Full/Oracle/Trimmed input modes — this yields genuinely useful diagnostic insights rather than a single leaderboard number.

Novel and valuable data-leakage analysis: manually obscured inputs for 20% of tasks quantify over-reliance on prior knowledge (12-16% fluctuation), a rarely addressed contamination concern for benchmark design.

Extensive evaluation: 8 LLMs across 18 DS-Guru configurations plus smolagents DR, OpenAI DR, and Gemini Agentic, with ablations on retrieval sampling, iterations, and runtime/cost reporting, plus a concrete failure analysis (fine-grained data-dependent reasoning, holistic data-lake understanding).
Strong reproducibility commitments: full artifacts (code, data, workloads, evaluation scripts, semi-automation scripts, reference system) stated to be publicly released.
weaknesses: Evidence for some central claims is inconsistent with the tables. The abstract claims retrieval is 'not the dominating obstacle' (only 9-10% gain from gold files), but Table 5 shows much larger Full-to-Oracle gaps for some systems (e.g., DS-Guru few-shot GPT-o3: 22.08% vs 31.92%), and Table 7 contains confusing cases where Obscured outperforms Oracle, undermining clean interpretation of the leakage analysis.

The pipeline-design evaluation relies on LLM-as-a-judge (CodeJudge-style) without reporting any validation of judge reliability against human judgment, yet headline claims (42% pipeline design) rest on it. Judge accuracy/bias should be measured for a benchmark paper.

Benchmark size and balance are modest: only 104 tasks, with heavily imbalanced domains (9 biomedical vs 30 legal tasks), which limits statistical strength of per-domain conclusions and the usefulness of per-domain rankings.

Contamination controls for closed-source systems are weak by the authors' own admission (internet restriction 'was not enforceable' for OpenAI DR and Gemini Agentic, and OpenAI DR's high Trimmed score is partly attributed to web search), yet these systems are compared alongside local, internet-off systems.

Signs of an unfinished manuscript: the reproducibility statement is missing the actual repository URL, Appendix B.2 contains leftover text ('We will update the paper to present these results...'), typos ('evaluade', 'wether'), and Appendix ablation tables (12-14) partially duplicate/conflict with Table 6, reducing confidence in the reported numbers.

Scoring choices are under-justified: partial-credit scoring like 1/(1+RAE) for numeric answers and F1 for lists may inflate end-to-end 'accuracy' numbers, and no sensitivity analysis of scoring scheme choices is provided. Table 1's benchmark comparison is also self-serving (e.g., marking DS-1000 as lacking data cleaning is debatable).

strengths: The benchmark targets a genuinely underexplored setting—end-to-end data-science pipelines over large, heterogeneous, noisy data lakes—which existing benchmarks (DS-1000, DSBench, BLADE, ScienceAgentBench) do not capture; the gap analysis in Table 1 is useful.
The task curation methodology is thoughtful: grounding tasks in published studies, cross-contributor validation, semi-automated sub-task/key-functionality generation with manual verification.
The three-level evaluation framework (end-to-end automation, pipeline design, sub-task implementation) provides diagnostic value beyond a single accuracy number.

The obscured-input experiment is a clever mechanism to probe memorization vs. data-dependent reasoning, and the failure analyses (clarification-seeking behavior, near-duplicate file confusion) yield interesting qualitative insights.
Broad coverage of systems: 18 DS-Guru configurations, smolagents DR with 4 LLMs, plus OpenAI DR and Gemini Agentic.
weaknesses: The submission is clearly unfinished/draft quality, which is disqualifying at a top venue: the reproducibility statement contains an empty repository link ('at The main paper section 2...'), a reference says 'Accessed: YYYY-MM-DD', Appendix B.2 contains leftover text 'We will update the paper to present these results...', and Table 15 is a verbatim duplicate of Table 2. For a benchmark paper whose primary contribution is a released artifact, an absent repository URL is a fundamental reproducibility failure.

Numerical inconsistencies and confusing claims throughout: the abstract says the best system reaches 50% end-to-end in the full setting, but Table 5's 'best' overall numbers mix Full (50%) and Trimmed (57.85%) settings; the Oracle result of 59% (Claude-3-7) contradicts the narrative that retrieval is 'not the dominating obstacle'; anomalies like GPT-4o Oracle wildfire = 0.002% are not explained or flagged.

No statistical rigor: single runs, no seeds, no confidence intervals or significance tests, despite small per-domain task counts (e.g., 9 biomedical tasks make the 44.44%/77.78% cells correspond to 4 and 7 tasks), so many reported differences are likely noise.

The pipeline-design metric relies on LLM-as-a-judge (Tong & Zhang 2024) with no validation of judge reliability (no human agreement study, no prompt details for the judge), and the ParaPluie 0/1 paraphrase scoring for string answers is similarly unvalidated—both directly affect headline numbers.

The closed-source DR evaluation is methodologically shaky: run manually through web UIs, internet access could not actually be disabled, and the Trimmed/Oracle* input modes (randomly subsampled gold sets) are not comparable across systems, weakening the headline comparisons.

The paper's insights (agentic flow helps; retrieval is not the bottleneck; fine-grained reasoning is weak) are largely predictable and partially undercut by its own data (e.g., Table 7's Obscured-vs-Full results are described with vague, speculative explanations), reducing scientific significance beyond the artifact itself.

Writing and presentation issues: duplicated content between Sections 2.2 and Appendix E, inconsistent model naming (GPT-o3 vs o3), inconsistent table schemas (Full/Trimmed/Oracle), and several grammatical errors suggest insufficient polish even beyond the missing artifacts.

strengths: KramaBench fills a genuine gap: it targets full data-lake-to-insight pipelines (data discovery, cleaning, integration, analysis) rather than isolated code generation or text-to-SQL, and Table 1 convincingly positions it against DS-1000, DSBench, BLADE, ScienceAgentBench, etc.

The benchmark is grounded in real-world published studies across 6 domains with 1700 files / 24 sources, and a disciplined 4-step curation workflow (independent cross-contributor validation, third-party reconciliation) lends credibility to reference solutions.

The three-tier evaluation design (end-to-end automation, pipeline design via key functionalities, sub-task implementation) is a thoughtful contribution in itself, enabling diagnostic attribution of failures rather than a single opaque accuracy number.
The obscured-input methodology for probing data leakage / memorization is a clever and underexplored evaluation angle, and the analysis of prior-knowledge effects (Table 7) is interesting.

Extensive empirical coverage: 8 LLMs, DS-Guru in 3 variants, smolagents DR, OpenAI DR, and Gemini Agentic, with input-mode ablations (Full/Oracle/Trimmed), retrieval-sample-size sweeps, iteration sweeps, runtime/cost reporting, and qualitative failure analyses.
Reproducibility and ethics statements are present, with artifacts (code, data, curation scripts, DS-Guru, evaluation scripts) promised in a public repository.
weaknesses: Statistical rigor is thin: all results appear to be single runs with no confidence intervals, seeds, or significance tests. Given LLM stochasticity and relatively small per-domain task counts (9–30 tasks), differences of a few points (e.g., 22.08% vs 24.68% in Table 6) may not be meaningful.

The pipeline-design setting relies entirely on LLM-as-a-judge (following CodeJudge) to determine whether a key functionality is 'covered' — this is the weakest link in the evaluation, and no human-verification or judge-accuracy analysis on a sample is provided. Judge noise could materially affect the 42% pipeline-design numbers.

Results contain internal inconsistencies that undermine confidence: e.g., DS-Guru few-shot GPT-o3 overall is 22.08% in Table 5 but 23.36% in Tables 12/14 for nominally the same 5-iteration configuration; Appendix B.2 reads as preliminary, informal notes ('We have started conducted ablation studies... We will update the paper'), and contradicts the claim that sampling more rows monotonically helps (Section 4.1 says performance does not meaningfully increase).

Closed-source deep research systems were evaluated manually through web interfaces with a non-enforceable 'no internet search' instruction and an arbitrary ≤10-file upload limit (Oracle* randomly sampling 10 gold files) — these design compromises make cross-system comparisons in the Trimmed setting hard to interpret fairly.

Some headline claims are stronger than the evidence: 'the best system reaches only 50% end-to-end accuracy' is presented as near-failure, but scoring gives continuous partial credit (e.g., 1/(1+RAE)); the sensitivity of conclusions to the scoring function (especially numeric-approximate and F1-based scoring) is not analyzed. It is also unexplained that end-to-end accuracy sometimes exceeds sub-task implementation accuracy (22% vs 19.75% for GPT-o3), which the paper notes but does not resolve.

Scale remains modest: 104 tasks and 20% obscured tasks, all in English and US-centric domains, limits statistical power for per-domain conclusions and generalizability; the authors themselves acknowledge language/cultural bias.

The DS-Guru reference framework and its OPS retrieval are fairly basic; conclusions about 'retrieval not being the dominant obstacle' may partially reflect the weakness of the OPS baseline rather than a property of agentic retrieval in general.

Writing and polish issues persist (garbled sentences in the intro, inconsistent naming of Claude models across tables, dangling repository URL in the reproducibility statement, citations with 'Accessed: YYYY-MM-DD'), suggesting the manuscript was not fully finalized.
